source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review: LLM-generated research ideas were rated more novel than expert-written ideas, slightly weaker on feasibility.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition; 79 reviewers, 298 reviews. Novelty mean (1-10, per review): human 4.84 (n=119), AI 5.64 (n=109), AI+human rerank 5.81 (n=109). Excitement 4.55 / 5.19 / 5.46. Feasibility 6.61 / 6.34 / 6.44 (not significant). Welch t-tests with Bonferroni.
quote: LLM-generated ideas are judged as more novel (p < 0.05) than human expert ideas
limits: Judged before any experiment was run. Ideas were style-normalised. Only NLP, prompting topics. Reviewer pool small and reviews are noisy (see c03).
agent_relevance: Idea generation is not the bottleneck; the pursuit decision is. Novelty judged at the ideation stage is cheap to produce and not proof of value.

source: Si et al. (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? (diversity analysis)
finding: Overgenerating ideas hits a diversity ceiling: most new ideas are near-duplicates of earlier ones.
numbers: Of 4000 seed ideas generated, only about 200 were non-duplicates (cosine similarity threshold 0.8). Non-duplicate share per batch falls as generation continues; accumulated unique ideas plateau.
limits: Duplicate test is embedding similarity at 0.8, set by manual inspection. One agent design, one model family.
agent_relevance: Samples from one model are not independent (G4). Sampling more ideas gives few new ones; dedup in code before spending budget on any.

source: Si et al. (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? (LLM judges and reviewer agreement)
finding: Humans agree with each other only a little above chance on idea quality, and LLM judges do worse than humans.
numbers: Inter-reviewer consistency 56.1% (random 50%). Best LLM evaluator, Claude-3.5 pairwise ranker, 53.3%. NeurIPS-2021 reviewer consistency cited as 66.0%. On ICLR submissions the same pairwise ranker got 71.4% (Claude-3.5-Sonnet zero-shot), GPT-4o 61.1%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%; few-shot and CoT gave no significant gain.
limits: Balanced top/bottom 25% agreement metric. Accepted-vs-rejected ICLR pairs are an easier task than ranking expert ideas.
agent_relevance: A preliminary-appraisal (Laudan pursuit) score from the model alone is weak. Treat it as a hint, never as the gate; spend a cheap real test instead.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: When experts actually executed the ideas, the LLM ideas lost their novelty advantage and ranked below human ideas on several metrics.
numbers: 43 experts, 100+ hours each, 4-page paper per project. N=19 human ideas, N=24 AI ideas. Score drop after execution: AI ideas -1.049 novelty, -1.760 excitement, -1.879 effectiveness, -1.976 overall; human ideas -0.010, +0.078, -0.052, -0.628. Difference in drops p=0.025 (novelty), 0.001, 0.003, 0.004 (FDR). After execution AI excitement 3.90 vs human 4.48; effectiveness 4.13 vs 4.78.
quote: a flip in rankings where human ideas score higher than LLM ideas
limits: Post-execution ranking flip itself is not statistically significant (small N). Executors modified ideas, but this explained only a small part of the gap. Correlation of ideation and execution scores is weak.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that appraisal-before-trying misleads for LLM ideas. Supports a gate that demands a cheap executed probe before committing budget, and distrust of the model's own pre-execution rating.

source: Si et al. (2025) Ideation-Execution Gap: review differences
finding: Ideation reviews rarely look at experiment design detail; execution reviews do. Part of the drop is because feasibility problems only show up once implemented.
numbers: Same N as c04. Controlling for idea changes during execution left AI ideas with significantly larger gaps (Appendix F).
limits: Qualitative review analysis of a small set.
agent_relevance: Preliminary appraisal should force concrete implementation detail (inputs, code path, data needed) before scoring; abstract ideas score too well.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Hypothesis Generation with Large Language Models (HypoGeniC)
finding: Generating hypotheses from data, then updating them with a bandit-style reward and a bank of wrong examples, beats zero-shot and few-shot prediction.
numbers: Over zero-shot: +60% SHOE SALES, +22.7% DECEPTIVE REVIEWS, +5.1% HEADLINE POPULARITY, +30.6% TWEET POPULARITY (averaged over LLMs). Over few-shot: +31.7%, +13.9%, +3.3%, +24.9%. Updating the hypothesis bank added on average 0.7%, 5.8%, 8.1%, 7.0% over no updates.
limits: Quality is measured as held-out classification accuracy, a narrow proxy for scientific value. Tweet popularity zero-shot inflated by safety refusals. Gains small on headline popularity.
agent_relevance: A working pursuit policy: score ideas on held-out data, spend budget on top-k by UCB-like reward, revise from failing examples. Fits G2/G3 (revise from real failures, test on held-out).

source: Zhou et al. (2024) HypoGeniC out-of-distribution
finding: Hypotheses learned on one dataset also transferred to out-of-distribution datasets, which is the check for fitting vs discovering.
numbers: Reported consistent gains on OOD datasets for deceptive reviews; fine-tuned models reach 100% on the synthetic set but not the real ones.
limits: Details of exact OOD numbers not recorded by this reader.
agent_relevance: Supports G3: a pass on data the hypothesis was not fitted to is the evidence that counts.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: Towards Data-Driven Discovery with Large Language Models
finding: Real data-driven discovery tasks are hard: the best agent-model pair scores only about 25%.
numbers: 264 real tasks (DB-REAL) plus synthetic (DB-SYNTH). Hypothesis match score (percent), DB-REAL: CodeGen 15.5/16.3/12.1 (GPT-4o/GPT-4p/Llama-3), ReAct 24.5/19.5/22.5, Reflexion with oracle feedback 14.1/8.7/10.9 as printed in the extracted table (columns hard to align). Replicating a paper's analysis took up to 90 person-hours, 30% did not reproduce.
quote: even the best system scores only 25%
limits: Table layout was garbled in text extraction, so per-cell attribution is uncertain; headline 25% is from the abstract. Outcome-based scoring by a GPT-4 evaluator.
agent_relevance: Baseline for whether an agent can find a true relation in data. Reasoning prompts (ReAct) and self-critic planning did not clearly help over simple CodeGen.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: NoDataGuess and feedback
finding: Self-critique planning did not help, but a real outcome signal (oracle score) did. Guessing the hypothesis without data tests memorisation.
numbers: NoDataGuess baseline scored 15.4/15.6/13.5 on DB-REAL for the three models in the extraction (GPT-4o refuses to guess). Authors state ReAct and DataVoyager do not improve CodeGen; Reflexion with oracle feedback significantly does.
limits: Oracle feedback is not available in real discovery.
agent_relevance: Matches G2: revision helps only with real external output, not with the model's own critique.

source: Beel, Kan, Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist for Autonomous Research
finding: An independent test of AI Scientist found weak novelty checking, frequent code failure and flawed or hallucinated results.
numbers: All 10 generated ideas and 2 seeds labelled novel, including well-known ones such as micro-batching and e-fold cross-validation. 5 of 12 experiments failed on coding errors (stated as 42%). Aider added on average only 8% more characters over iterations. 4 of 7 manuscripts (57%) had hallucinated or incorrect numbers, missing figures or placeholder text.
limits: Small sample (12 ideas, 7 manuscripts), one template domain (recommender / training efficiency), earlier AI Scientist version.
agent_relevance: Novelty gate by keyword search against literature fails. S0 and pursuit gates need an actual retrieval with reading, and a code check of results.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
finding: End-to-end loop of idea, novelty check, experiment, write-up and automated review, at low cost; the LLM reviewer matches human reviewers on accept/reject balanced accuracy.
numbers: Under $15 per paper. Automated reviewer 65% vs human 66% balanced accuracy on ICLR 2022 OpenReview. Review cost $0.25 to $0.50. Review ensembling of 5 reviews did not change performance but lowered variance. Cheaper models (Sonnet 3.5, GPT-4o-mini) reviewed substantially worse.
limits: Evaluation against ICLR data may have contamination; self-reported. Beel et al. (c10) found serious defects in practice.
agent_relevance: Idea gate in this system: model scores interestingness, feasibility, novelty, but only the 'novel' label gates later steps (see c10). A cautionary design.

source: Yamada et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search
finding: Adds best-first tree search over experiment nodes chosen by a scalar score; one of three fully AI-written papers passed workshop review.
numbers: 3 papers submitted to an ICLR workshop; best average reviewer score 6.33 (reviews 6, 7, 6), about top 45% of submissions. The paper itself reported a negative result (compositional regularization gave no significant gain).
limits: Workshop level, 3 papers, authors' own report. Authors withdrew after review. No claim of main-conference quality.
agent_relevance: Tree search that picks which node to refine next by an external score is a pursuit policy already in use. Note it needs a measurable score (validation metric).

source: Wen, Zhang et al. (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
finding: Models can be trained to say which of two research ideas will work better, and beat human experts, but only after fine-tuning.
numbers: Off-the-shelf GPT-4.1 51.9%; o3 near chance. Fine-tuned GPT-4.1 (6,000 historical idea pairs) 77% on the full test set. NLP subset: system 64.4% vs 25 human experts 48.9%. Fresh post-cutoff test: 63.6%. Retrieval of full papers (not abstracts) lifted accuracy from 38.8% to 53.0%. Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 gained only 45.0% to 53.7%. Chain-of-thought fine-tuning gave no gain.
limits: Pairs come from published work, so selection effects. 77% is on in-distribution test; the clean fresh set gives 63.6%. Human baseline is only 25 experts.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that pursuit appraisal can be learned. Without training, zero-shot appraisal is at chance, which argues against trusting an unscaffolded model to pick ideas.

source: Yang, Liu, Cambria et al. (2024/2025) Large Language Models for Automated Open-domain Scientific Hypotheses Discovery / MOOSE-Chem: LLMs for Rediscovering Unseen Chemistry Scientific Hypotheses
finding: Decomposes discovery into retrieve inspirations, compose hypothesis, rank hypotheses; retrieval of the right inspiration papers is surprisingly accurate.
numbers: Benchmark of 51 chemistry papers from 2024 (post cutoff). More than 75% of ground-truth inspirations are covered by only 4% of the chosen corpus. Screening window 15, keep 3, two rounds: 4% of corpus kept, hit ratio 83.7%; a variant keeping 5% got 71.6%.
limits: Hit ratio is overlap with the paper's known inspirations; does not prove the final hypothesis would be true. Authors' 'latent associations' claim is speculative.
agent_relevance: A heuristic strategy (Darden-style: find analogs or inspirations, then compose) works for an LLM, and it narrows the search cheaply.

source: Huang, Leskovec et al. (2025) Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications (POPPER)
finding: Turns a hypothesis into several measurable implications, tests each by an agent, and combines p-values (e-values) sequentially so Type-I error is controlled.
numbers: Six domains; alpha 0.1. Plain baselines such as Self-Refine had Type-I error 0.248 on DiscoveryBench; ReAct 0.145 there; POPPER-CodeGen variants above 0.3 on some sets. POPPER reported valid error control with power 0.610 (DiscoveryBench) and 0.897 (TargetVal-IL2). Claims comparable accuracy to human scientists on biology hypotheses with 10x less time.
limits: Table extraction partially garbled; cell attribution uncertain. Human comparison is on a small set of biology hypotheses.
agent_relevance: A pre-pursuit cheap falsification gate with a stopping rule. Agent self-checks inflate false positives; a statistical wrapper fixes this.

source: Wang et al. (2023) SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty
finding: Iteratively comparing a generated idea with retrieved related work and asking for revision raises novelty; baseline GPT-4 ideas are low in depth and novelty.
numbers: Novelty iteration: 1st round raised novelty for 54.4% of ideas (GPT4FS), 55.6% (+SN), 47.8% (+CT), 46.7% (+KG); 2nd round raised it for 57.8% of those continued. Versus the original paper's idea, the real idea was judged higher in technical level and novelty in 85% of comparisons.
limits: Small human annotation study on scientific abstracts; 2023 models.
agent_relevance: A working novelty-check loop: retrieve, compare, rewrite, stop on a threshold. Still far below real ideas (85%).

source: Shojaee, Ruan et al. (2025) LLM-SR: Scientific Equation Discovery via Programming with LLMs
finding: LLM proposes equation skeletons, data fits constants, results are fed back as evolutionary memory; generalises out of domain far better than symbolic regression baselines.
numbers: Best out-of-domain NMSE about 0.0037 on one task while other methods exceeded 1 (read from text snippet).
limits: Only grep-level reading of results; benchmark tasks are physics and biology with known forms, so recall of known equations is a confound.
agent_relevance: Heuristic discovery strategy with external fit as the selector, which is the pursuit rule that works in domains with a score.

source: Ruan et al. (2024-2026) Evaluating LLMs' Divergent Thinking Capabilities for Scientific Idea Generation with Minimal Context (LiveIdeaBench)
finding: Idea-generation quality from single keywords is poorly predicted by general intelligence scores.
numbers: Over 40 models, 1,180 keywords, 22 domains, five dimensions (originality, feasibility, fluency, flexibility, clarity) rated by an LLM panel. QwQ-32B-preview reported comparable creative performance to a top model.
limits: Only abstract and header read; LLM-panel judging inherits biases in c03.
agent_relevance: Choose the ideation model separately from the reasoning model; do not assume stronger reasoners give more original ideas.

source: Tang, Zhang et al. (2025) AI-Researcher: Autonomous Scientific Innovation (Scientist-Bench)
finding: Full pipeline from literature review to paper with a benchmark of guided and open-ended tasks; authors report high implementation completeness.
numbers: 93.8% completeness rate with Claude-series models; failures in complex technical cases. Test-time scaling by refinement cycles raised implementation success.
limits: Self-reported by the system authors; completeness is about running code, not about the idea being correct. Not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Implementation success is not discovery success (compare c04). Use it as a throughput number only.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) LLMs are zero-shot hypothesis proposers
finding: Early test that LLMs can propose hypotheses from background knowledge and a few observations; precursor to HypoGeniC.
numbers: Downloaded and title confirmed only; no numbers read.
limits: Not read beyond the title.
agent_relevance: Pointer for later reading.

source: Langley, Simon, Bradshaw, Zytkow (1987) Scientific Discovery: Computational Explorations of the Creative Process (BACON, GLAUBER, STAHL, DALTON)
finding: Older AI systems that rediscover laws by heuristic search over data: BACON found Kepler, Ohm, ideal gas style laws by trying product and ratio terms when a variable is constant or monotone.
numbers: From memory, no numbers verified this session.
limits: Not opened; rediscovery from already-cleaned data, so hindsight advantage. Covered in the sibling folder 06 on machine discovery.
agent_relevance: Heuristic rules as discoverability tests (cheap heuristic: is there a monotone or constant relation?) are a precedent for an S0 gate. Link only.

source: Darden (2006) Reasoning in Biological Discoveries; Schaffner (1993) Discovery and Explanation in Biology and Medicine
finding: Strategies for anomaly resolution and for building mechanisms: schema instantiation, modular subassembly, forward and backward chaining on a mechanism schema.
numbers: None verified; not opened.
limits: Philosophy of science case studies; no controlled test of use by LLMs found in this search.
agent_relevance: Schema instantiation maps to our idea of filling a typed slot in a mechanism template; no LLM test of this exact method was found.

source: Lu et al. (2024) AI Scientist, idea generation prompt design
finding: Ideas must carry self-scored interestingness, feasibility and novelty fields, and a literature search with Semantic Scholar sets a binary novel flag.
numbers: Per Beel et al. (c10): only the binary novel flag affects later workflow; the numeric scores are not used downstream.
limits: Reading of the Beel analysis plus the AI Scientist text; not a measured experiment on the scores.
agent_relevance: Self-scores that do not feed any decision are noise. Make pursuit depend on measured, code-computed quantities.

source: Cross-study synthesis (Si 2024, Si 2025, Wen 2025) comparison: appraisal accuracy versus outcome
finding: Across c01, c03, c04, c13, human and LLM appraisal of ideas before execution is weak: pairwise agreement 53 to 56%, ideation-execution score correlation weak, fine-tuned predictor 63.6 to 77%.
numbers: c03: 56.1% human, 53.3% best LLM judge. c04: weak Pearson and Spearman correlation between ideation and execution scores (Appendix D, values not recorded). c13: 63.6 to 77% only after fine-tuning.
limits: A synthesis by this reader across different tasks and metrics; not one study.
agent_relevance: Laudan-style pursuit appraisal can only be trusted when anchored to outcomes. A scaffold should log which idea features predicted success in its own runs, rather than rely on prior judgement.

source: Si et al. (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? (pipeline design)
finding: The generation baseline combines retrieval of papers, massive overgeneration, dedup and Swiss-tournament pairwise ranking; ranker separates top and bottom ICLR papers.
numbers: Retrieval up to N=120 papers. Swiss rounds N=5 chosen. Average ICLR review score, top-10 vs bottom-10 by ranker: gap 0.56 (1 round), 0.90, 0.97, 0.95, 1.73 (6 rounds), as read from Table 1 (one row garbled).
limits: Ranker validated on ICLR papers, not on idea-stage proposals; human rerank added only a small gain (novelty 5.64 to 5.81).
agent_relevance: Rank by code-run tournament with pairwise comparisons, not by absolute model scores. More rounds help to a point (G5).

source: Si et al. (2024) related-work note on human novelty judgement
finding: Authors flag that expert novelty judgement itself is hard, and propose follow-up execution studies.
numbers: Referenced prior: normalisation approaches gave 50% accuracy for expert human judges (line 194 of the extracted text).
limits: Single sentence in related work, source of the 50% figure not traced.
agent_relevance: Do not use a single human or model novelty rating as ground truth for tuning the scaffold.
